title: Fake News on the Farm: How Misinformation Shapes Cocoa Farmers' Decisions in Jukwa, Ghana
screen_reason: Cross-sectional survey of 390 cocoa farmers in the Jukwa cocoa district, Ghana. Table 5 reports a share of respondents with a clear denominator: 177/390 (45.4%) answered Yes to 'Experience of misinformation', i.e. having acted on cocoa farming information that later proved false. That is a self-reported encounter with false information expressed as a share of respondents, so RECALL. The paper's aim (decision-making, susceptibility factors) is something else, but the descriptive share is reported.

estimates.country: Ghana (Jukwa cocoa district, Central Region; zones Jukwa, Abura-Dunkwa, KEEA)
estimates.platform: face-to-face survey (CAPI, KoboCollect); no single media platform
estimates.measure_type: % of surveyed cocoa farmers who reported having acted on cocoa farming information that later proved false
estimates.denominator: 390 cocoa farmers in the Jukwa cocoa district (multi-stage sample drawn from a district population of 16,129 farmers)
estimates.definition: Respondent answered Yes to having acted on cocoa farming information that later proved false. Note this is a stricter numerator than simple exposure: the farmer must have acted on the information, not merely encountered it, so it is a floor on self-reported exposure.
estimates.misinfo_def: "misinformation, defined as false or misleading information (Van der Meer & Jin, 2020)"
estimates.source_quote: Nearly half of the surveyed farmers (45.4%) reported having acted on cocoa farming information that later proved false
estimates.page_loc: Results and discussion, 'Farmers' experience of misinformation in cocoa farming'; Table 5
estimates.ground_truth_detail: The respondent's own retrospective judgement that farming information they acted on later proved false; no external verification and no coder reliability. The authors' limitations section states: 'The data relied heavily on self-reported perceptions of misinformation. Such perceptions may be influenced by recall bias, misclassification of accurate information as misinformation, or the reluctance of respondents to admit adopting practices later considered harmful.'
estimates.moderator_quote: The study population consisted of all the cocoa farmers (16,129) in the study area. The sample size for the study was statistically representative, based on 95% confidence level and 5% error margin. It was determined following Yamane's formula for sample size calculation (Yamane, 1967), thus, 390 farmers.
estimates.notes: The Table 5 cell backing this row reads 'Experience of misinformation / Yes 177 45.4 / No 213 54.6'; the quoted span is the sentence in the Results text, cut before a hyphenated line break in the text file. Topic coded 'other' (agricultural/agronomic information: pruning, pricing, fertilizer, pest control), which no listed topic category covers. population_scope coded 'professional' because the sample is defined by occupation (smallholder cocoa farmers interviewed about farming information), not a general-population sample; an adjudicator may prefer general_public since these are rural households rather than a credentialed profession. Neither the data-collection period nor the publication year appears in the text; year 2025 is taken from the latest works in the reference list and is therefore a publication-year approximation, not a stated collection date. The Conclusion says 'nearly half (45.5%)' while the Results text and Table 5 both say 45.4% (177/390 = 45.38%); the table value is used.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Types of misinformation experienced (pruning 67 = 37.6%, cocoa pricing 59 = 33.1%, fertilization 40 = 22.5%, pest management 35 = 19.7%, etc., Table 5) are a multiple-response breakdown computed inside the 177 farmers who reported misinformation, i.e. a topic profile of the misinformation, not a further prevalence share, so no rows. (2) Sources of misinformation (other farmers 154 = 87.0%, cooperatives 38 = 21.5%, radio/TV 27 = 15.3%, social media 13 = 7.3%, extension officers 12 = 6.8%, Table 5) are likewise a within-misinformation channel breakdown of the same 177 respondents, not a share of a population or of items. (3) Consequences of misinformation-driven practices (Table 7: reduced yield 57 = 80.3%, etc.) are outcomes, and the reported percentages do not match a denominator stated anywhere in the paper (57/80.3% implies about 71, which is neither 177 nor 390); not extracted, and the mismatch is flagged. (4) Information-verification practices (52.0% consult an extension officer, 16.4% do not verify) are behaviour, not misinformation exposure. (5) The logistic regression (Table 6) gives odds ratios for susceptibility, not shares. (6) Source-use shares (extension officers 96.4%, radio/TV 52.8%, social media 19.5%) describe information access generally, not misinformation.

rob.design: Cross-sectional face-to-face survey. Frame: all 16,129 cocoa farmers in the Jukwa cocoa district; multi-stage selection (district purposively chosen; three zones with proportionate allocation of 85/197/108; communities randomly selected; farmers randomly selected from district-office lists), n = 390 sized by Yamane's formula at 95% confidence and 5% margin. Structured questionnaire translated into the local language, pre-tested, administered by CAPI (KoboCollect) with daily data checks. No response rate, no refusal count and no test-retest or inter-rater reliability reported; the misinformation measure is entirely self-reported and the authors acknowledge recall bias and misclassification.
rob.item6_quote: However, this expanded information landscape has also amplified the circulation of misinformation, defined as false or misleading information (Van der Meer & Jin, 2020).
rob.item10_quote: Nearly half of the surveyed farmers (45.4%) reported having acted on cocoa farming information that later proved false, highlighting the vulnerability of the sector to misinformation (Table 5).
